rows.title: Potential for Automated Imaging Analysis in Facial Aesthetics
rows.abstract: Dear Editor, I am writing to bring to your attention to the innovative potential of ChatGPT-4 (Open AI, San Francisco, CA, USA) in the realm of automated imaging analysis for facial aesthetics. ChatGPT-4 is the latest iteration of OpenAI’s Generative Pre-Training Transformer, a language model that uses deep learning to produce human-like text. ChatGPT has the ability to answer questions, tell stories, write web code, and even form concepts and ideas about extremely complicated topics (Gordon et al., 2024). I wish to highlight its application in distinguishing between sinker and sagger facial aging patterns. Individuals who are sinkers are characterized by fat compartment atrophy, especially within the lateral-temporal cheek fat compartments, which leads to a sunken facial appearance. Individuals who are saggers exhibit signs of fat repositioning from the midface to the lower third of the face that results in tissue drooping, bulging, and increased wrinkle formation (Swift et al., 2021). Recent studies have demonstrated the utility of ChatGPT and similar artificial intelligence (AI) models in various imaging applications, including medical image segmentation, radiology, and dermatological analysis (Esteva et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020). For example, ChatGPT has been used to support automated diagnosis in radiographic imaging, identifying abnormalities with significant precision. Moreover, in dermatology, AI-based tools are able to detect and classify skin lesions from images, improving diagnostic accuracy and providing invaluable assistance to clinicians in early cancer detection (Li et al., 2022). These examples underscore the potential of ChatGPT-4 in analyzing facial imaging, not only for assessing facial aging characteristics but also for broader applications across aesthetic and medical fields. By harnessing these technologies, practitioners can improve both the precision of diagnostic assessments and the quality of patient care. This advancement aligns with insights from a recently published article titled Profhilo® Structura, Current Status and Future Perspectives: A Practical Review (Forte et al., 2024) that discusses the role of adipose tissue depletion and redistribution in facial aging. ChatGPT-4 presents a promising tool to further enhance the precision of facial imaging analysis and evaluation. Moreover, the app can be installed on any smartphone, enabling practitioners to conduct these analyses conveniently and flexibly during patient consultations. Further, ChatGPT-4, allows practitioners to develop specific prompts that can quantify and assess sinker or sagger characteristics in facial images. Such analysis could provide significant utility in aesthetic practices. Following is a predefined prompt that practitioners can copy and paste as a proposed approach for performing this imaging analysis: Analyze facial imaging to quantify the degree of sinker or sagger characteristics by evaluating fat compartment depletion, volume loss, and tissue sagging in the middle and lower third of the face. The analysis should express results as a percentage of sinker and sagger features based on anatomical and aesthetic criteria. Facial Region Identification: Segment the face into the following anatomical regions: lateral-temporal cheek, zygomatic area, nasolabial region, and jowl. Sinker Characteristics: Quantify the extent of fat depletion and hollowness in the lateral-temporal and preauricular areas, identify signs of volume loss leading to sunken cheeks, and calculate the percentage of facial surface area affected by fat loss and sunken appearance in the midface. Sagger Characteristics: Analyze the sagging or drooping of tissue, particularly in the jowl and lower third of the face, evaluate the shift or redistribution of fat from the zygomatic area to the lower face, and measure the degree of tissue laxity, ptosis, and bulging, focusing on the midface and jowl regions. Percentage Calculation: Assign a percentage score for sinker characteristics based on the degree of fat loss and hollowing, assign a percentage score for sagger characteristics based on the extent of tissue sagging and fat redistribution, and based on a visual assessment of the provided images and the outlined criteria, estimate an approximation of the sinker and sagger characteristics (e.g., 60% sagger, 40% sinker). To ensure consistent and accurate results, it is crucial that the images used for analysis meet specific standards of clarity and zoom, similar to those generated by the Canfield Scientific imaging systems (Parsippany, NJ, USA) and QuantifiCare (Suwanee, GA, USA). These qualities include maintaining a consistent distance, lighting, and resolution to capture detailed facial features and fat compartments. In cases where the quality of the images is suboptimal and the ChatGPT-4 is unable to generate a score, the practitioner can still proceed with the analysis by using the following prompt: Approximate score based on visible features. This approach allows for a degree of flexibility in cases where the image quality might hinder the automated analysis, ensuring that even lower-quality images can still provide valuable insights. Based on visual assessments of 60 images (utilizing both front and 45-degree views), the ChatGPT-4 has demonstrated the capacity to effectively evaluate facial aging with an accuracy of 0.775 (77.5%). These preliminary results suggest that ChatGPT-4 could become a valuable asset to aesthetic medicine, particularly for pretreatment assessments. Given that Profhilo® Structura (IBSA Farmaceutici Italia, Lodi, Italy) targets fat compartment atrophy and tissue sagging, this novel AI-driven imaging analysis could serve as a powerful tool for aesthetic physicians by streamlining patient evaluations, improving treatment planning, and offering a precise approach to facial rejuvenation, which is especially relevant in the context of hyaluronic acid-based treatments such as Profhilo® Structura. Incorporating AI technologies such as ChatGPT-4 into routine practice could not only enhance patient outcomes but also support physicians in making more data-driven decisions. Furthermore, this integration would align well with current advancements in aesthetic medicine, fostering more accurate predictions of treatment outcomes and potentially accelerating the adoption of such technologies within clinical practice. Sincerely, Luciano Lanfranchi, MDPlastic SurgeonDepartment of Plastic and Reconstructive SurgeryCentro Diagnostico ItalianoMilan, Italy

rows.title: Assisted artificial intelligence in medical writing: a primer for humans
rows.abstract: Assisted artificial intelligence (A-AI) has rapidly become a gold standard approach for conducting data analysis and medical writing [1]. From executing complex statistical tasks to extracting relevant information and supporting manuscript drafting, A-AI is increasingly embedded in the daily workflow of clinical and translational researchers [2]. However, the thin red line between being assisted by AI and becoming reliant on it, or even fully driven by it, is becoming harder to define. This ambiguity raises essential questions about authorship, accountability and the integrity of scientific output in the AI era. A growing number of early-career researchers are engaging with high-dimensional machine learning (ML) methodologies, often without comprehensive training in classical statistics or computational foundations. While the integration of such advanced tools reflects a welcome shift towards data-driven research, it also raises concerns regarding methodological rigor. In certain instances, traditional statistical frameworks are overlooked, and AI-generated outputs, particularly those derived from large language models, are interpreted without sufficient critical appraisal. To better understand this, 2 examples of A-AI analysis follow. To assess the magnitude of post-procedural thrombocytopaenia after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) and its potential interplay with subclinical leaflet thrombosis (SLT) as detected by 1-month multidetector computed tomography (MDCT), I turned to my ‘Assisted AI master’. Within seconds, the AI generated a synthetic dataset comprising 100 patients and 120 prespecified variables, including demographic, procedural and post-implantation metrics, based on the assumption that SLT would occur in 18% of the sample. To enhance realism, I requested a ‘real-world’ dataset with missing values and statistical outliers. My AI master not only accommodated these nuances but also proposed appropriate imputation strategies, including multiple imputation by chained equations. My assisted AI master returned the following dataset (synthetitic.csv) with the variables reported in Fig. 1 [3]. AI master was instructed to perform multiple imputation to address missing data. Variables’ name and description provided as synthetic data. Once the dataset was imputed, the AI executed an ML pipeline using the popular Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) algorithm to predict SLT [4]. Without any need for custom code or manual feature engineering, the model was trained and internally validated. To enhance interpretability, the AI automatically produced the R-code for a beeswarm plot of SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values, offering a visually compelling summary of the model’s top predictors and their direction of effect [5]. Within moments, a complete set of analytical outputs is provided and easily be mistaken for a results section ready for submission of for an abstract, for example (Fig. 2A). By interpreting the SHAP beeswarm plot, my A-AI master concluded that ‘Age’ was the most influential variable driving the model’s prediction of SLT. The entire process took only a few min. While the dataset is entirely synthetic, it remains a valuable resource for statistical training and method development. Both the dataset and the full R code are available for download in the public repository (https://github.com/mmlondon77/Biobook.). (A) SHAP plot showing which synthetic features have the biggest impact on the model’s predictions. (B) Forest plot of odds ratio by a multivariable logistic regression. BMI: body mass index; SHAP: SHapley Additive exPlanations. We aimed to explore whether colchicine is effective in preventing SLT at 1 month following TAVI. To do so, I turned to my AI master, and within min, a complete synthetic randomized clinical trial (RCT) was generated. The simulated RCT included 200 patients, randomized 1:1 to receive colchicine or placebo. Baseline and procedural variables were generated to reflect clinical realism, including: age, sex, body mass index (BMI), valve type (balloon-expandable or self-expanding), preoperative and postoperative platelet counts, Delta platelet drop (a marker of post-TAVI thrombocytopaenia), postoperative creatinine and bleeding complications. The primary end-point was the presence of SLT detected by multidetector CT (MDCT) at 1 month. The expected incidence of SLT was set at 30% in the placebo group and 15% in the colchicine group. A multivariable logistic regression confirmed the effect: patients in the placebo group had significantly higher odds of developing SLT compared to those receiving colchicine (adjusted OR 5.6, 95% CI 2.45–12.8, P< 0.001), even after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, valve type and key procedural variables. What once required months of trial infrastructure and patient recruitment was now simulated, statistically sound, fully documented, and ready for analysis, in just a few min (Fig. 2B). The 2 examples reported above are intentionally simple and naïve, yet effectively demonstrate how rapidly AI can operate in the context of medical data analysis and scientific writing. Unsurprisingly, AI systems are now capable of generating far more complex synthetic datasets and corresponding manuscripts with increasing sophistication. There are some obvious risks with that. Opacity in authorship attribution: It is becoming increasingly difficult to discern the extent to which a manuscript has been generated by a human author versus an AI system. This lack of transparency challenges traditional notions of authorship, intellectual contribution, and accountability. Loss of analytical oversight: With the proliferation of AI-assisted data analysis tools, the control over analytical choices—such as model selection, assumptions testing and sensitivity analyses, is increasingly being delegated to algorithms. In many cases, researchers may not fully understand or critically evaluate the processes that led to the reported results. Bias amplification and misinterpretation: AI models, particularly those trained on large datasets without proper curation, may inadvertently propagate existing biases or generate misleading associations. Without expert oversight, spurious correlations may be reported as meaningful findings, distorting scientific conclusions [6]. Reproducibility and validation challenges: Many AI-generated analyses, especially those involving complex pipelines or proprietary algorithms, lack sufficient documentation to allow independent replication. This undermines a core principle of scientific research: reproducibility. Ethical and regulatory ambiguity: The accelerated integration of A-AI in research has outpaced the development of clear ethical guidelines and regulatory frameworks. Questions remain regarding data ownership, informed consent in AI-driven secondary analyses and appropriate disclosure of AI contributions in publications. Fabrication potential and misuse of synthetic data: AI tools now make it relatively easy to generate synthetic datasets that mimic real-world data [3]. While this can be useful for simulation or training purposes, the same tools can be misused to fabricate results that appear statistically sound but are entirely artificial. This creates new challenges for peer reviewers, editors and regulators tasked with validating the integrity of submitted research. Are we, as researchers, becoming obsolete? Can we still compete with the sheer ‘brute force’ of AI? By brute force, I mean the machine’s ability to analyse millions of potential patterns in moments, something no human can match. Consider chess. Stockfish (https://stockfishchess.org/), a leading chess engine built on alpha–beta pruning, is far more powerful than newer models like DeepSeek or even ChatGPT. It can evaluate billions of positions and calculate with ruthless precision. No human can match that computational depth. Yet humans bring something different intuition. The ability to feel the right move without calculation. To reach the same brilliant conclusion as Stockfish, not through search trees, but through instinct and insight. In medical research, we may no longer outperform AI in pattern recognition or speed. But the value of a well-formulated research question, of clinical intuition, of knowing what truly matters that remains uniquely human. If AI is the engine, then intuition must be the compass. This concept is rapidly becoming obsolete. The penetration of AI into the research process is no longer theoretical; it is already here, quietly embedded in literature searches, data cleaning, analysis pipelines and even the phrasing of sentences. Insisting on a rigid declaration of where ‘human input’ ends and ‘AI contribution’ begins may give the illusion of transparency, but in reality, the line is increasingly meaningless. The boundaries between human reasoning and machine assistance are dissolving. Is using AI to impute missing data different from using it to draft an introduction? Is grammar correction less artificial than code generation? Attempting to fence off human and machine contributions might once have made sense. Now, it risks becoming a distraction. The focus should shift: not who wrote the words or ran the code, but how responsibly, transparently and reproducibly the research was conducted. We are witnessing a proliferation of ‘mega journals’, not to mention the rise of predatory outlets, where the time from submission to online publication is often astonishingly short. As shown above, generating a synthetic paper or accelerating the analysis and writing process is now trivially easy with A-AI. While this can be useful for simulation or education, it also opens the door to a flood of potentially biased or low-quality publications, polluting the scientific literature. This raises a provocative question: should we deploy A-AI not just for authorship, but for peer review as well? Are we entering an era of machine versus machine, where algorithmic authors face off against algorithmic reviewers? At the end of the day, can a human truly compete with AI in spotting every flaw, inconsistency or statistical misstep? And more importantly, should we even try? Amid the flood of A-AI–generated science, patients may begin to question: Where does the truth lie? Who is behind the words they read in medical reports, trials, or treatment guidelines? And this, from a physician’s perspective, may be one of the greatest shadows of artificial intelligence, not the automation itself, but the erosion of trust. Trust that the knowledge is grounded in real experience. Trust that what is written was not merely generated, but truly understood. One of the most critical and underappreciated risks in the increasing use of A-AI is what aviation psychology describes as the out-of-the-loop performance problem (OOPP) [7]. Coined by Raja Parasuraman in 1997, this phenomenon occurs when human operators lose situational awareness and manual proficiency due to prolonged reliance on automation. When the system fails or abruptly relinquishes control, the human is cognitively and operationally unprepared to take over. In medicine, a parallel risk is emerging. As A-AI becomes more embedded in data analysis, diagnostics and manuscript generation, researchers and clinicians may gradually lose the ability—or confidence—to critically re-engage with raw data, statistical assumptions or narrative construction. Much like in aviation, where the safety of the flight ultimately depends on the pilot’s readiness to step in, the integrity and originality of scientific research may hinge on our ability to remain ‘in the loop’, despite the growing sophistication of the tools we use. Artificial intelligence did not descend from Mars. Its roots stretch back to early 20th-century thinkers who laid the intellectual groundwork for what we now call machine intelligence. It is uncertain whether Alan Turing ever said, ‘One day ladies will take their computers for walks in the park and tell each other, “My little computer said such a funny thing this morning.”’ Still, it is a charming image, and fitting, in spirit (Fig. 3). Turing (1912–1954) is widely regarded as the father of AI. In his seminal 1950 paper ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’, he asked a deceptively simple question: Can machines think? This led to the formulation of the Turing Test, a framework for evaluating machine intelligence, not by its internal workings, but by its behaviour [8]. Another example stems from Corrado Gini (1884–1965), an Italian economist, statistician and early socialist thinker. Best known for the Gini coefficient, a measure of inequality in income or wealth distribution, Gini developed mathematical tools to evaluate and correct disparities within societies [9]. Originally rooted in social justice and economic fairness, his work has since been reappropriated into modern computational contexts. In ML, the Gini importance (also known as mean decrease in impurity) is a fundamental metric used in decision tree algorithms like Random Forests (Fig. 4). It determines how much each feature contributes to reducing uncertainty when making splits in the tree, a far cry from its origins in wealth redistribution. English Heritage blue plaque marking the building where Alan Turing was born, located in Little Venice, London. Photo taken by M. Moscarelli, 2018. Random Forest for predictors using Gini Coefficient applied to synthetic data. Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in clinical research workflows, from data processing and modelling to manuscript drafting. While the human role remains essential—particularly in hypothesis formulation, clinical interpretation and ethical oversight—it is becoming more supervisory, curatorial or interpretive. In this context, the term AI-assisted medical writing may no longer be appropriate. A more accurate description reflects the reality of human-assisted machine research, where the computational workload is largely executed by algorithms under human direction. Acknowledging this inversion is essential to ensure transparency, methodological integrity and proper attribution in modern scientific communication. This study received no specific funding. Conflict of interest: The authors report no conflicts of interest. The GIROC is a task force of the Italian Society for Cardiac Surgery aimed to encourage, support and coordinate independent studies in the cardiac surgery community. We thank all the members of GIROC: L. Di Marco (Division of Cardiac Surgery, IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna, Italy), A. Nenna (Unit of Cardiac Surgery, Ospedale “Maggiore della Carità” di Novara, Novara, Italy), A. Salsano (Division of Cardiac Surgery, Ospedale Policlinico San Martino, Genoa, Italy DISC Department, University of Genoa, Genoa, Italy) and G. Santarpino (Department of Cardiac Surgery, Città di Lecce Hospital, GVM Care & Research, Lecce, Italy). All code used for data generation, analysis and figure production—including the synthetic examples shown in this manuscript—is openly available in the corresponding author’s GitHub repository: https://github.com/mmlondon77/Biobook. rows.title: What’s New in Hip Replacement
rows.source: Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery
rows.abstract: About 19% of patients with degenerative joint disease awaiting a total hip arthroplasty (THA) experience a health state worse than death. Pain is the main contributing factor1. Reducing the burden of completing complicated patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) remains a challenge. A possible alternative is the use of a modified Single Assessment Numerical Evaluation (M-SANE). This 1-question PROM was shown to perform similarly to multiple-question PROMs among patients undergoing primary THA2. Implant Design and Related Outcomes Cemented Compared with Cementless Stem Fixation In a recent study on 1,671 Medicare patients undergoing primary THAs during a 4-year span (2014 to 2017), cemented femoral fixation outperformed cementless fixation, with a significantly higher likelihood of discharge home and a trend toward a shorter length of stay and lower readmission rate, cost of care, and reoperation rate3. A Norwegian Arthroplasty Register study based on 66,995 THAs from 2005 to 2017 also found the highest risk of revision in elderly women (≥55 years of age) receiving cementless stems, mainly due to periprosthetic fracture and dislocation4. Highly Cross-Linked Polyethylene (HXLPE) A long-term follow-up (mean, 16 years) of a prospectively collected cohort of 237 patients <50 years of age demonstrated significantly less wear-related revision and higher survivorship in the HXLPE group compared with the non-HXLPE group5. The evidence from the National Joint Registry for England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man (NJR) revision data set indicated that the best survival at a 12-year follow-up was observed in THAs utilizing polyethylene liners subjected to a total radiation dose between ≥5 Mrad and <10 Mrad, followed by remelting, and incorporating an asymmetrical face. An irradiation dose of ≥10 Mrad showed no further risk reduction6. Ceramic-on-Ceramic or Ceramic-on-Polyethylene Design Two long-term follow-up studies (minimum, 15 years) on a ceramic-on-ceramic design and/or ceramic-on-polyethylene design demonstrated no sign of osteolysis based on radiographic or computed tomographic (CT) imaging7,8. The baseline ceramic fracture rate in the contemporary ceramic-on-ceramic design was also investigated. In a Level-I meta-analysis study, Yoon et al. reported a lower rate of ceramic fracture in the delta group (0.2%) compared with the forte group (0.5%). Also, the ceramic fracture rate per 1,000 patient-years was 0.5 for the delta group and 0.9 for the forte group. The ceramic head fracture rate was 0.1% for the delta group compared with 0.2% for the forte group9. Dual-Mobility Construct A Level-III propensity score matching study from the Nordic Arthroplasty Register Association (NARA) demonstrated that the use of a dual-mobility construct as primary treatment for hip fracture (4,520 hip fractures) was associated with an overall lower risk of revision, especially due to dislocation10. The conclusion of the study ought to be interpreted with caution, as a majority of the THAs were performed via a posterolateral approach and there was an overall higher mortality rate with a dual-mobility construct (40.1%) than with a conventional cup (26.6%)10,11. In another study, 100% survivorship at 10 to 16 years was reported, using a contemporary dual-mobility construct design with hydroxyapatite coating. No dislocations, revisions, or osteolysis were observed. However, there was a very high number of patients lost to follow-up (167 of 310 died before 10 years)12. Reduced rates of dislocation were also found in a dual-mobility construct compared with a conventional bearing in a retrospective case-control study among 267 revision THA cases done via anterior and lateral approaches at an intermediate-term follow-up (24 to 73 months)13. Patient Factors in Relation to Outcomes Not all patients recover at the same rate. A Level-III prognostic study from the Dutch joint registry (6,030 patients) identified 3 subgroups of patients with different functional recovery trajectories after THA: fast starters (87.7%), slow starters (4.6%), and late dippers (7.7%)14. Female patients and patients who smoked tended to be slow starters, and older age (>75 years), obesity, higher American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grades (III or IV), worse EuroQol-5 Dimensions (EQ-5D) scores, cemented acetabular implants, and a direct lateral approach were risk factors for the late dipper category. An anterior approach was protective against a less favorable response14. Young Patients Excellent clinical outcome scores and survivorship could be expected in patients who were ≤20 years of age at an intermediate-term to long-term follow-up using modern implants15. Race and Ethnicity A prognostic Level-III study of Kaiser Permanente universally insured patients found similar or lower rates of lifetime reoperation and 90-day postoperative events in minority patients compared with white patients, and black and Hispanic patients had higher rates of 90-day emergency department visits16. Medical Comorbidities Medical comorbidities including preoperative malnourishment (albumin, <3.4 g/L), polycythemia vera, preoperative anemia (even as mild as hematocrit of 27% to 36%), Parkinson disease, and dementia usually have a negative impact with regard to THA outcomes17-21. However, a history of prostate cancer did not increase the risk of short-term complications after THA22. The in-hospital mortality for patients with Parkinson disease was not increased according to a matched cohort study from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS)19. Patients undergoing dialysis who are on a transplant list should delay an arthroplasty until the transplant has taken place to minimize complications. For patients undergoing total joint arthroplasty (TJA), researchers found a significantly higher rate of postoperative complications (especially surgical site infection and periprosthetic joint infection) among patients undergoing dialysis at 18% compared with the renal transplant group at 3.5%. Patients in the dialysis group also had a higher rate of revision at 24% than patients in the transplant group at 3.5%. Patients in the dialysis group had lower survivorship than patients in the transplant group23. The 5-year mortality rates following primary THA were 62.6% for patients undergoing renal dialysis, 37.3% for patients undergoing a kidney transplant, and 15.0% for patients with non-renal disease. Patients undergoing dialysis and those undergoing a transplant are high-risk groups, with significantly increased 90-day readmission incidences of 55% for patients undergoing dialysis and 43% for patients undergoing a transplant, making it challenging to include them into a bundled payment model24. Patients with a lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and especially those with <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, are more likely to sustain medical complications and have a mortality rate 6 to 9 times higher than those with a normal estimated GFR undergoing primary THA25. For those patients who were dialysis-dependent because of end-stage renal disease, the peritoneal dialysis group had a significantly lower risk of periprosthetic joint infection compared with the hemodialysis group26. A prognostic matched case-control study showed that the 15-year cumulative risk of revision was closely related to the etiology of osteonecrosis, ranging from 25% to 0% for idiopathic, steroid-induced, posttraumatic, alcohol-induced, and radiation-induced etiologies in descending order27. Prior Hip Arthroscopy In patients with a diagnosis of osteoarthritis who underwent hip arthroscopy, Malahias et al. found unacceptably high rates of conversion to THA (up to 68.4%) within 2 years. Additionally, following conversion to THA, those patients faced a significantly increased risk of revision within 2 years after the index THA28 (odds ratio [OR], 3.72 [95% confidence interval (CI), 3.15 to 4.57]; p = 0.012). The conversion group was also found to have increased surgical time and increased perioperative complications29. Prior Femoral Osteotomy There is no clear evidence to support the practice of staged implant removal to mitigate the risk of intraoperative fracture or subsequent infection, although the conversion surgical procedure is technically more demanding and may carry a higher risk of complications30. Body Mass Index (BMI) An Australian meta-analysis and systematic review study of 2,190,824 patients found that obese and morbidly obese patients remained at a higher risk of complications after THA, especially deep infection31. This was supported by a Dutch study of 218,214 THAs that showed that the ASA score and BMI (especially >40 kg/m2) were the strongest predictors for 1-year revision. BMI and previous hip surgical procedure were independent risk factors for revision after 3 years32. Spine Pathology In candidates for THA, flatback deformity (estimated 16%) and hyperlordosis (estimated 25%) are quite common33. Although patients with prior spine fusion had a lower self-reported physical activity level compared with patients without spine fusion both before and after THA, both groups saw a similar degree of improvement in physical activity level following THA34. Preoperative Opioid Use Preoperative opioid use continues to be an area of active research. Vakharia et al. demonstrated, in a matched control analysis of 42,097 patients with Medicare, that patients with opioid use disorder were at greater risk to experience implant-related complications, periprosthetic joint infections, and readmissions and had higher costs following primary THA compared with patients without opioid use disorder35. Bonner et al. also reported significantly lower PROMs, longer hospital stays, and a more likely discharge to rehabilitation in this population36. Surgical Factors in Relation to Outcome Surgical Approach In a recent American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons (AAHKS) online survey, over one-half (56.2%) of 996 total respondents currently perform the direct anterior approach37. A multicenter, prospective study of 3,018 participants found a dramatic PROM score improvement at 6 months following THA regardless of the surgical approach (posterior, transgluteal, and anterior)38. This was supported by a Mayo Clinic study showing similar 30-day major and minor complications regardless of the surgical approach employed (direct anterior, lateral, and posterior)39. Another multicenter, prospective, international study using propensity score matching found no superior early postoperative PROM scores (1.5 months postoperatively) in patients who underwent a THA performed with a direct anterior approach compared with those who underwent a THA performed with a posterolateral approach. No PROM differences were found at ≥1 year up to 5 years40. A large, retrospective study of 16,186 consecutive THAs investigated the early mechanical complications (within 2 years of the surgical procedure) using 3 different approaches: 5,465 using the direct anterior approach, 8,561 using the direct lateral approach, and 2,160 using the posterolateral approach41. The adjusted risks of instability within 2 years were 0.17% for the direct lateral approach, 0.74% for the direct anterior approach, and 1.74% for the posterolateral approach. Femoral component failure, including fracture or loosening, occurred more frequently for the direct anterior approach (1.20%) compared with the direct lateral approach (0.58%) and the posterolateral approach (0.47%). The direct lateral approach seemed to have the lowest overall risk of mechanical complications41. Another retrospective study of the NJR using propensity score matching reported similar 5-year survivorship free of revision for dislocation between the posterior and anterolateral approaches, and lower risks of mortality and intraoperative complications when treating patients with a femoral neck fracture with a posterolateral approach42. Complications According to a retrospective study of 4,555 primary cementless THAs from a single institution, wound-related complications remained the most common reason for reoperation, followed by periprosthetic fracture and pain; dislocation and acute periprosthetic joint infection accounted for a total of 79% of revision procedures involving an isolated exchange of at least 1 modular implant (head or liner)43. Venous Thromboembolism and Anticoagulation Approximately 1 in 167 patients undergoing THA develops venous thromboembolism within 30 days after a surgical procedure. The reported rates of venous thromboembolism following THA were stable between 2008 and 201644. Glassberg and Lachiewicz demonstrated an increase usage of rivaroxaban, and a decrease in warfarin use, after elective THA among commercially insured (23,768 patients) and Medicare beneficiaries (12,155 patients) between 2010 and 2015. Although there was a similar risk of bleeding, warfarin users were more likely to experience deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism than rivaroxaban45. Osteolysis and Aseptic Loosening The practice of using radiostereometric analysis (RSA) for monitoring implant migration to predict long-term stability of cementless implants has recently been questioned. Frazer and Tanzer reported only 6 of the initial 9 stems with “anticipated stability” had favorable survivorship at the 10-year follow-up, and 1 of 2 initially poor performing stems according to RSA actually did well at 10 years46. Close surveillance of patients with an Exactech Connexion GXL liner was recommended following the observation of 12 cases of early postoperative failure due to wear and severe osteolysis at a single institution in addition to the 22 cases reported to the Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience database from 2009 to 2019. A unique “polar-locking” mechanism on the back side of the liner seemed to be the cause47. Dislocation Numerous studies on standard precautions compared with relaxed or no posterior precautions after THA via a posterolateral approach showed no difference in the risk of dislocation48,49. rows.abstract: OCCUPATIONAL OPTOMETRY: HOW CAN OPTOMETRISTS INTEGRATE IT INTO EYE CARE DELIVERY FOR INDUSTRIES? As workplaces continue to evolve – from tech-driven offices to labor-intensive industries – the visual demands placed on workers are increasing in complexity and risk. This talk addresses the emerging role of occupational optometry in supporting visual health across formal and informal work environments and how optometrists can strategically integrate this specialty into industrial eye care delivery. Occupational optometry is now gaining formal recognition as a specialized domain under the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions (NCAHP). This inclusion not only validates its clinical and public health importance but also opens new pathways for optometrists to collaborate with occupational health systems, government agencies, and industries at large. The presentation will explore: • The scope and components of occupational optometry as outlined in the NCAHP • How optometrists can partner with industrial stakeholders to conduct workplace visual task analyses, implement ergonomic interventions, and create custom vision correction strategies • The potential for early detection and prevention of occupation-related visual disorders, thereby reducing absenteeism, injuries, and productivity loss • Crucially, this talk also highlights the urgent and often overlooked needs of workers in the unorganized sector, who are typically excluded from structured occupational health programs • This talk aims to reframe the optometrist’s role – not just as a clinician but as a proactive partner in promoting workplace safety, productivity, and equity in vision care access. Dr. Rashima Professor and Head Elite School of Optometry and The Sankara Nethralaya Academy, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India. ESTABLISHING THE QUALITY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM IN A DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORY Quality management system (QMS) in a clinical laboratory is a structured framework that ensures the accuracy, reliability, and timeliness of test results. It includes all components of the laboratory, including organizational structure, processes, and procedures to maintain consistent quality and support continual improvement. Components of a Laboratory Quality Management System include: 1. Organization and Leadership: To define the roles, responsibilities, and accountability within the laboratory 2. Customer Focus: To ensure that laboratory services meet the needs and expectations of patients and healthcare providers 3. Facilities and Safety: To maintain a safe and conducive environment in the laboratory 4. Personnel: Competent staff 5. Inventory Management: A system to alert us to procure the required consumables on time 6. Equipment: To select, maintain, and calibrate laboratory equipment 7. Process Management: Standardized procedures for preanalytical, analytical, and postanalytical phases of testing 8. Document control and control and retention of the records: Preparation of the quality documents, their amendments, storage, and accessibility. Maintenance of timely and accurate records 9. Laboratory Information Management System: Validated by the manufacturer and verified by the users. LIMS is linked to HIMS for accurate and safe data transfer, ensuring uninterrupted systems for efficient information flow 10. Continual improvement: To allow staff to identify nonconformity in the laboratory and bring it to the knowledge of the Quality Manager. Later, to take necessary corrective and preventive measures along with an internal audit at least every year. Dr. Niranjan Gopal, Additional Professor, Department of Biochemistry, AIIMS, Nagpur, Maharashtra, India. HEMODYNAMIC MONITORING DURING RESUSCITATION Resuscitation is a dynamic and time-sensitive process, often involving rapid shifts in a patient’s hemodynamic status. Continuous monitoring is essential to guide therapy, assess response, and optimize outcomes. Effective hemodynamic monitoring allows clinicians to tailor interventions such as fluid therapy, vasopressors, and inotropes to the patient’s evolving needs. Goals of Hemodynamic Monitoring The ultimate goal during resuscitation is to restore and maintain: preload: the volume of blood returning to the heart, contractility: the force of myocardial contraction, and afterload: the resistance to forward blood flow in the arterial system. Achieving balance among these three components ensures adequate tissue perfusion, which is the cornerstone of successful resuscitation. Techniques of Hemodynamic Monitoring Monitoring methods can be broadly categorized into clinical, noninvasive, minimally invasive, and invasive techniques. The choice of tools depends on equipment availability, clinician expertise, and the clinical setting. 1. Clinical Assessment: These bedside indicators provide immediate clues about perfusion status: pulse rate and volume, skin temperature and color, capillary refill time, level of consciousness, and urine output 2. Noninvasive Monitoring: electrocardiogram: monitors heart rate and rhythm, non-invasive blood pressure: measures blood pressure (BP) noninvasively, SpO₂: pulse oximetry for oxygen saturation, EtCO₂: end-tidal CO₂ for monitoring ventilation and CPR effectiveness, and point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS): cardiac function, lung status, and inferior vena cava (IVC) variability 3. Invasive Monitoring: arterial line: continuous BP monitoring and arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling, central venous pressure (CVP) measurement, pulmonary artery catheter (PAC) for advanced parameters, and blood gas analysis: ABG and venous samples to assess perfusion 4. Dynamic Assessment of Fluid Responsiveness: Stroke volume variations, pulse pressure variation, and systolic pressure variations, IVC diameter variation: collapsibility/distensibility index, and PLR test: passive leg raise to mimic fluid bolus effect. Conclusion: Effective resuscitation requires timely recognition and management of hemodynamic instability. A combination of clinical signs, noninvasive and invasive tools, and dynamic assessment techniques allows individualized and goal-directed resuscitation. Integrating these modalities improves outcomes by ensuring adequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery. Dr. Mohan, Additional Professor, Department of Anaesthesia,JIPMER, Puducherry, India. PACEMAKERS EXPLAINED: TECHNOLOGY, USES, AND IMPACT ON HEART HEALTH Basic Introduction for Allied Health Professionals Pacemakers are life-saving medical devices designed to correct abnormal heart rhythms, or arrhythmias, particularly bradycardia (a slow heart rate). As allied health professionals, having a foundational understanding of how pacemakers work and their role in patient care is essential, especially as cardiac technologies continue to evolve. The heart relies on its conduction system to beat regularly and efficiently. Electrical impulses begin in the SA node, then travel through the atrioventricular node and into the ventricles via the His-Purkinje system. When this system malfunctions, the heart may beat too slowly, irregularly, or inefficiently, leading to symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue, or fainting. Pacemaker Technology: How It Works A pacemaker helps maintain proper heart rhythm by delivering electrical impulses when the heart intrinsically fails to do so on its own. It includes: • Pulse Generator: A small, battery-powered unit implanted under the skin near the clavicle (collarbone). It generates electrical signals • Leads: Thin, insulated wires that carry signals from the generator to the heart muscle. There are several types of pacemakers: • Single chamber: Stimulates one heart chamber (usually the right ventricle) • Dual chamber: Provides synchronous contraction of both the atrium and ventricle • Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy: Used primarily in heart failure patients to synchronize the contraction of both ventricles. Conduction System Pacing: “Physiological way of Pacing” Traditional pacemakers stimulate the heart muscle directly (right ventricular apex), which can cause dyssynchrony over time, leading to pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. Conduction System Pacing is an advanced technique that stimulates the heart’s natural conduction system, such as the His bundle or the left bundle branch. Impact on Patient Care and Allied Health Roles Patients with pacemakers often lead full, active lives, but the presence of a device requires awareness in clinical settings. For allied health professionals: • Always confirm if a patient has a pacemaker before imaging or procedures (e.g., Magnetic resonance imaging, and diathermy) • Monitor for signs of malfunction (e.g., fatigue, irregular pulse, and dizziness) As frontline healthcare providers, allied health professionals play a key role in implantation, following up, and troubleshooting these devices. Mr. Mohamed Akram K A CEPS., CCDS., FHRS., Highly Specialised Cardiac Physiologist, United Kingdom. rows.title: Focus on device innovation in interventional cardiology and on trials in cardiovascular prevention
rows.abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Focus Issue on interventional cardiology and clinical trials contains the Special Article entitled ‘Device innovation in cardiovascular medicine: a report from the European Society of Cardiology Cardiovascular Round Table’ by Stephan Windecker from the University of Bern, and colleagues.1 The authors note that research performed in Europe has driven cardiovascular device innovation. This includes, but is not limited to, percutaneous coronary intervention, cardiac imaging, transcatheter heart valve implantation, and device therapy of cardiac arrhythmias and heart failure. An important part of future medical progress involves the evolution of medical technology and the ongoing development of artificial intelligence and machine learning. There is a need to foster an environment conducive to medical technology development and validation so that Europe can continue to play a major role in device innovation while providing high standards of safety. Devices are developed and improved through an iterative process throughout their life cycle. Early feasibility studies demonstrate proof of concept and help to optimize the design of a device. If successful, this should ideally be followed by randomized clinical trials comparing novel devices vs. accepted standards of care, when available, and the collection of post-market real-world evidence through registries. Unfortunately, standardized procedures for feasibility studies across various device categories have not yet been implemented in Europe. Cardiovascular imaging can be used to diagnose and characterize patients for interventions, to improve procedural results and to monitor devices long term after implantation. Randomized clinical trials often use cardiac imaging-based inclusion criteria, while less frequently trials randomize patients to compare the diagnostic or prognostic value of different modalities. Applications using machine learning are increasingly important, but specific regulatory standards and pathways remain in development in both Europe and the USA. Standards are also needed for smart devices and digital technologies that support device-driven biomonitoring. Changes in device regulation introduced by the European Union aim to improve clinical evidence, transparency, and safety, but they may impact the speed of innovation, access, and availability. Device development programmes including dialogue on unmet needs and advice on study designs must be driven by a community of physicians, trialists, patients, regulators, payers, and industry to ensure that patients have access to innovative care. This paper summarizes viewpoints on the topic of device innovation in cardiovascular medicine at the European Society of Cardiology Cardiovascular Round Table, a strategic forum for high-level dialogue to discuss issues related to the future of cardiovascular health in Europe. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become a viable treatment option for patients with severe aortic valve stenosis across a broad range of surgical risk.2–7 The Nordic Aortic Valve Intervention (NOTION) trial was the first to randomize patients at lower surgical risk to TAVI or surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR). In a Fast Track Clinical Research article entitled ‘Transcatheter or surgical aortic valve implantation: 10-year outcomes of the NOTION trial’, Hans Gustav Hørsted Thyregod from the Copenhagen University Hospital in Denmark, and colleagues report clinical and bioprosthesis outcomes after 10 years.8 The NOTION trial randomized 280 patients to TAVI with the self-expanding CoreValve (Medtronic Inc.) bioprosthesis (n = 145) or SAVR with a bioprosthesis (n = 135). The primary composite outcome was the risk of all-cause mortality, stroke, or myocardial infarction. Bioprosthetic valve dysfunction (BVD) was classified as structural valve deterioration (SVD), non-structural valve dysfunction (NSVD), clinical valve thrombosis, or endocarditis according to Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 criteria. Severe SVD was defined as (i) a transprosthetic gradient of 30 mmHg or more and an increase in transprosthetic gradient of 20 mmHg or more or (ii) severe new intraprosthetic regurgitation. Bioprosthetic valve failure (BVF) was defined as the composite rate of death from a valve-related cause or an unexplained death following the diagnosis of BVD, aortic valve re-intervention, or severe SVD. Baseline characteristics were similar between TAVI and SAVR: age 79 and 79 years, male 53% and 54%, and Society of Thoracic Surgeons score <4% of 83.4% and 80.0%, respectively. After 10 years, the risk of the composite outcome of all-cause mortality, stroke, or myocardial infarction was 65% after both TAVI and SAVR, with no difference for each individual outcome. Severe SVD occurred in 1.5% and 10.0% [hazard ratio (HR) 0.2; P = .02] after TAVI and SAVR, respectively. The cumulative incidence for severe NSVD was 20% and 43% (P < .001) and for endocarditis 7.2% and 7.4% (P = 1.0) after TAVI and SAVR, respectively. No patients had clinical valve thrombosis. BVF occurred in 9.7% of TAVI and in 13.8% of SAVR patients (HR 0.7; P = .4) (Figure 1). Clinical and bioprosthesis 10-year outcomes after transcatheter or surgical aortic valve implantation. TAVI, transcatheter aortic valve implantation; SAVR, surgical aortic valve replacement. Hazard ratio (HR); 95% confidence interval (CI); the P-value was based on Cox regression.8 Thyregod and colleagues conclude that in patients with severe aortic stenosis and lower surgical risk randomized to TAVI or SAVR, the risk of major clinical outcomes is not different 10 years after treatment. The risk of severe bioprosthesis SVD is lower after TAVR compared with SAVR, while the risk of BVF is similar. The contribution is accompanied by an Editorial by Sabine Bleiziffer from the Herz- und Diabeteszentrum Nordrhein-Westfalen in Bad Oeynhausen, Germany.9 Bleiziffer concludes that the NOTION 10-year data confirm current European Guideline recommendations that TAVI in low-risk patients above the age of 75 is indicated and has equal long-term outcomes compared with SAVR. Long-term data on the durability of specific transcatheter and surgical prosthesis types in younger patients are still lacking and will be essential for differentiated decision-making in younger patients. Physical activity plays an important role in cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention.10–15 In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Aerobic, resistance, or combined exercise training and cardiovascular risk profile in overweight or obese adults: the CardioRACE trial’, Duck-chul Lee from Iowa State University in Ames, IA, USA, and colleagues sought to determine the comparative efficacy of resistance, aerobic, and combined resistance plus aerobic exercise on CVD risk profile.16 This randomized controlled trial enrolled 406 adults aged 35–70 years with overweight or obesity and elevated blood pressure (BP). Participants were randomly assigned to resistance (n = 102), aerobic (n = 101), combined resistance plus aerobic exercise (n = 101), or no-exercise control (n = 102). The primary outcome was the change from baseline to 1 year in the standardized composite Z-score of four well-established CVD risk factors: systolic blood pressure (SBP), LDL cholesterol, fasting glucose, and per cent body fat. Among 406 participants (53% women), 94% completed 1-year follow-up. Compared with the control group, the composite Z-score, which indicates an improved CVD risk profile, significantly decreased at 1 year in the aerobic (P = .01) and combination (P = .009) groups, but not in the resistance group, while there was no difference between the aerobic and combination groups. The authors conclude that in adults with overweight or obesity, aerobic exercise alone or combined resistance plus aerobic exercise, but not resistance exercise alone, improves composite CVD risk profile compared with the control. The contribution is accompanied by an Editorial by Martin Halle from the Technical University of Munich in Germany and Michael Papadakis from the University of London in the UK.17 The authors highlight that the management of obesity has been a domain of diabetology and nutrition medicine. Now it has reached cardiology and will remain there. The introduction of the optimal exercise and lifestyle programme in addition to medication for overweight and obese subjects with or without diabetes will be a key challenge for the multidisciplinary obesity and metabolic team. Therefore, a clear educational strategy on obesity and obesity-associated diabetes management for the general cardiologist is essential, which is already on the preventive cardiology curriculum of the European Association of Preventive Cardiology. Effective management of obesity provides an important addition to the armamentarium of preventive cardiology that should benefit many hundreds of millions of patients worldwide. Management of cardiovascular disease before non-cardiac surgery is highly debated.18–20 Haemodynamic instability is associated with peri-operative myocardial injury, particularly in patients receiving renin–angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin II receptor blockers). In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Discontinuation vs. continuation of renin–angiotensin system inhibition before non-cardiac surgery: the SPACE trial’, Gareth Ackland from the Queen Mary University of London in the UK, and colleagues note that it remains unclear whether stopping RAS inhibitors to minimize hypotension, or continuing RAS inhibitors to avoid hypertension, reduces peri-operative myocardial injury.21 From 31 July 2017 to 1 October 2021, patients aged ≥60 years undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery were randomly assigned to either discontinue or continue RAS inhibitors prescribed for existing medical conditions in six UK centres. RAS inhibitors were withheld for different durations (2–3 days) before surgery, according to their pharmacokinetic profile. The primary outcome, masked to investigators, clinicians, and patients, was myocardial injury assessed by measuring plasma high-sensitivity troponin-T (hs-TnT) before and within 48 h after surgery. Pre-specified adverse haemodynamic events occurring within 48 h of surgery included acute hypertension (>180 mmHg) and hypotension requiring vasoactive therapy. Two hundred and sixty-two participants were randomized to continue or stop RAS inhibitors. Myocardial injury occurred in 48% of patients randomized to discontinue, compared with 41% of those randomized to continue (P = NS). Hypertensive adverse events were more frequent when RAS inhibitors were stopped (12.4% vs 5.3%), while hypotension rates were similar (9.3% vs. 8.4%) (Figure 2). In a randomized controlled trial enrolling 260 patients, did stopping renin–angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors [angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-I)/angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB)] before elective non-cardiac surgery reduce myocardial injury, taking into account the pharmacokinetic profile of individual RAS inhibitors? Pre-operative blood pressure was higher when RAS inhibitors were stopped. Forty-eight per cent of patients sustained myocardial injury after stopping RAS inhibitors, compared with 41% of patients who continued therapy. Hypertensive adverse events were more frequent when RAS inhibitors were stopped, without affecting hypotension rates. Discontinuing RAS inhibitors before non-cardiac surgery does not appear to reduce myocardial injury, and could increase the risk of clinically significant acute hypertension.21 The authors conclude that discontinuing RAS inhibitors before non-cardiac surgery does not reduce myocardial injury, and could increase the risk of clinically significant acute hypertension. This manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by W. Scott Beattie from the University of Toronto in Canada.22 Beattie concludes by noting that there are now eight randomized trials investigating the efficacy of interventions to limit the adverse effects of peri-operative hypotension. Whether the intervention is notification of hypotension, early warning from an artificial intelligence algorithm, maintaining a higher intra-operative pressure with inotropes, or the pre-operative withdrawal of a potential hypotensive medication, there is no evidence that these strategies are superior to an anaesthesiologist responding to routine monitoring. With respect to RAS inhibitors, there are now two independent randomized trials showing that withdrawal of pre-operative RAS inhibitors neither limits the incidence or severity of intra-operative hypotensive episodes nor decreases adverse outcomes. There is, however, a suggestion that withdrawing RAS inhibitors increases the chance of harm. The evidence suggests that the major cardiovascular societies need to re-visit their recommendations on the disposition of peri-operative RAS inhibitors. Visit-to-visit systolic blood pressure variability (BPV) is an important predictor of cardiovascular outcomes. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Legacy benefits of blood pressure treatment on cardiovascular events are primarily mediated by improved blood pressure variability: the ASCOT trial’, Ajay Gupta from the Queen Mary University of London in the UK, and colleagues indicate that morbidity and mortality follow-up of UK participants in the Anglo-Scandinavian Cardiac Outcomes Trial-Blood Pressure-Lowering Arm has been extended for up to 21 years to determine the cardiovascular impact of mean SBP control and BPV during the trial, and amongst those allocated to amlodipine- and atenolol-based treatment.23 More than 8500 hypertensive participants assigned to amlodipine ± perindopril-based or to atenolol ± diuretic-based treatment during the in-trial period (median 5.5 years) were followed for up to 21 years. In-trial mean SBP and standard deviation of visit-to-visit SBP as a measure of BPV were measured using >100 000 BP measurements. Using BP data from the in-trial period, in the post-trial period, although mean SBP was a predictor of cardiovascular outcomes (P < . 001), systolic BPV independent of mean SBP was an even stronger predictor of cardiovascular events (P < .001) and predicted events even in participants with well-controlled BP. During 21-year follow-up, those on amlodipine-based compared with atenolol-based in-trial treatment had significantly reduced risk of stroke (P = .003), total cardiovascular events (P = .008), total coronary events (P = .024), and atrial fibrillation (AF; P = .03), with weaker evidence of a difference in cardiovascular mortality (P = .073). There was no significant difference in the incidence of non-fatal myocardial infarction and fatal coronary heart disease, heart failure, and all-cause mortality. The authors conclude that systolic BPV is a strong predictor of cardiovascular outcome, even in those with controlled SBP. The long-term benefits of amlodipine-based treatment compared with atenolol-based treatment in reducing cardiovascular events appear to be primarily mediated by an effect on systolic BPV during the trial period. The contribution is accompanied by an Editorial by Gianfranco Parati, Grzegorz Bilo, and Alessandro Croces from the IRCCS Istituto Auxologico Italiano in Milan, Italy.24 The authors note that BPV appears at least non-inferior to other emerging cardiovascular risk factors listed in recent international guidelines for cardiovascular prevention and hypertension management. Its association with outcomes appears as strong as that of, for example, lipoprotein(a), birthweight, or air pollution. At variance from BPV, many of these factors have no formal evidence supporting their ability to reclassify risk. Moreover, accumulating evidence suggests that a specific pharmacological intervention can modify BPV. In contrast, many factors listed in the guidelines such as arterial stiffness or air pollution are not easily or not at all modifiable on an individual level. On such a background and given the results of the study by Gupta et al., the moment may thus have finally arrived to seriously consider use of BPV in clinical practice as an additional BP-related, potentially modifiable risk factor. The issue also contains a Rapid Communications contribution entitled ‘Icosapent ethyl following acute coronary syndrome: the REDUCE-IT trial’ by Neila Sayah from the Hôpital Bichat in Paris, France, and colleagues.25 The authors note that the REDUCE-IT [Reduction of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl (IPE)-Intervention Trial] trial showed robust reductions in ischaemic events with IPE vs. placebo, including reduced cardiovascular death, albeit with increased rates of bleeding, and of AF. Patients with recent (<12 months) acute coronary syndrome (ACS) are at very high risk of future cardiovascular events (including arrhythmias) for which they usually receive intensive antithrombotic therapy, which might increase bleeding risk with IPE. The benefit and safety of IPE in this specific patient subgroup are largely unknown and were explored in the present post-hoc analysis of the original trial database. The authors found that IPE dramatically reduced the risk of ischaemic events in high-risk, statin-treated patients with recent ACS without excess bleeding. The authors conclude that these findings support initiation of IPE in REDUCE-IT-eligible patients as soon as possible after ACS. The issue is also complemented by two Discussion Forum contributions. In a commentary entitled ‘To transplant or not to transplant “marginal” donor hearts: is machine perfusion the answer?’, Jorik Amesz, Olivier Manintveld, and Yannick Taverne from Erasmus University Medical Center in Rotterdam, the Netherlands comment on the recent publication ‘Disparities in donor heart acceptance between the USA and Europe: clinical implications’ by Brian Wayda from the Stanford University School of Medicine in California, USA, and colleagues.26,27 Wayda et al. respond in a separate comment.28 The editors hope that this issue of the European Heart Journal will be of interest to its readers. Dr. Crea reports speaker fees from Abbott, Amgen, Astra Zeneca, BMS, Chiesi, Daiichi Sankyo, Menarini outside the submitted work. With thanks to Amelia Meier-Batschelet, Johanna Huggler, and Martin Meyer for help with compilation of this article.

rows.abstract: Acceptability and Feasibility of Implementing Intraoperative Autotransfusion in Kenya Naeema Hopkins-Kotb, BS, Isita Tripathi, BS, Nikathan Kumar, MD, Abdirahman M Jibrail, BS, Cindy Makanga, MA, Caroline W Wangamati, MS, MA, Asma A Awadh, MBBS, MHM, MIPH, Tecla Chelagat, PhD, MPH, Nakul Raykar, MD, FACS Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA; University of California, San Francisco - East Bay, Oakland, CA; Turkana County Government Department of Health, Lodwar, Kenya; Strathmore University Business School, Nairobi, Kenya; Blood Desert Coalition, Nairobi, Kenya; Office of Health for Langata and Kibera Sub-Counties, Nairobi, Kenya; Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA Introduction: Intraoperative autotransfusion (IAT) presents a useful strategy to improve blood access, particularly in regions without consistent supply. However, its implementation has not been explored in hospitals with limited blood banking infrastructure. We aimed to identify the barriers and facilitators to introducing a low-cost, manual filtration IAT device across 3 low-resource sites - 2 rural and 1 urban - in Kenya. Methods: We conducted 17 semi-structured interviews with healthcare providers and administrators in Lodwar, Nairobi, and Kilifi, Kenya. Interviews were transcribed using artificial intelligence-assisted software and reviewed for accuracy. Transcripts were systematically coded using an iterative thematic analysis approach. An inter-rater reliability of 82% was achieved after consensus-coding 5 interviews, and the remaining 12 interviews were independently coded. Results: All respondents highlighted the utility of IAT technology in mitigating community blood access challenges. Key barriers to implementation included device procurement (n = 14) and maintenance (n = 9), clinical situations precluding IAT use (n = 10), and data collection and monitoring (n = 1). Key facilitators included training (n = 16) and sensitization of staff (n = 12), and patient perception of the device (n = 14). Interprofessional communication was identified as both a barrier and facilitator (n = 9). See Figure 1. Conclusion: Integrating IAT devices would be feasible and acceptable across 1 urban and 2 rural sites in Kenya. Implementation efforts should prioritize obtaining administrative buy-in for sustainable device procurement and maintenance, using hospital metrics to validate use, developing protocols for documentation and establishing indications for IAT use.Figure 1Association Between Undergoing Formal Preoperative Risk Assessment and Postoperative Complication Haaris Kadri, BA, William G Henderson, MPH, PhD, Yi Su, MPS, Yaxu Zhuang, Micaella R Zubkov, MD, Kathryn L Colborn, PhD, MSPH, Robert A Meguid, MD, FACS University of Colorado School of Medicine, Aurora, CO Introduction: Few studies have evaluated associations between use of formal preoperative risk assessment and postoperative complication. Methods: This was a propensity-matched observational study using electronic health record data from 5 hospitals, 2017-2024. The validated Automated Surveillance of Postoperative Infectious and Non-Infectious Complications (ASPIN) system was used to calculate complication occurrence probabilities. A propensity model was developed using logistic regression. 1:1 Greedy matching was used to match patients who had and did not have the Surgical Risk Preoperative Assessment System (SURPAS) used before operation. After matching, cohorts were compared for estimated rates of 13 different postoperative complications. Results: Of 457,003 patients, 22,875 patients (5.0%) had SURPAS. The SURPAS group was older, had more patients with American Society of Anesthesiologists class 3-4, fewer with emergent operation, and more with 2+ comorbidities than the non-SURPAS group. The average standardized mean difference (SMD) = 0.2479. The propensity model’s c-index = 0.8673 and Brier Score = 0.0429. After propensity matching, both cohorts had 22,642 patients. The matched average absolute SMD = 0.0245. In comparing 13 postoperative complications, the only large differences were a lower mortality rate (3.79% vs 4.51%), but higher rate of overall morbidity (7.08% vs 6.51%) and non-home discharge (18.27% vs 15.27%) for SURPAS-exposed patients, all p < 0.001. Conclusion: It is possible that SURPAS identifies high-risk patients leading to modification of processes of care associated with reduced mortality and increased referral to non-home discharge in order to improve patient recovery. The absence of change in other complications may be due to lack of recommended process of care focused at reducing complication in high-risk patients. Association of Hospital Integrated Private Medicare Insurance with Surgical Complication and Outcomes Alexander P Philips, BS, Geronimo Bejarano, MPH, David J Meyers, MPH, PhD, Thomas C Tsai, MD, MPH, FACS Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University, Providence, RI; Brown University School of Public Health, Providence, RI; Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA Introduction: Consolidation of hospitals with privatized Medicare through Medicare Advantage (MA) plans has grown. Hospital-MA vertical integration (VI) may enable better care coordination and improved outcomes through aligned financial and clinical incentives. However, evidence on its impact on surgical outcomes remains limited. This study evaluates the association of patient insurance coverage to vertically integrated hospital-MA plans and surgical outcomes. Methods: This serial cross-sectional study analyzed 2,119,340 inpatient surgical admissions in MA from MEDPAR for 2015-2022 in colectomy, coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), cystectomy, hysterectomy, peripheral bypass, pulmonary lobectomy, total hip arthroplasty, and total knee arthroplasty. Admissions were categorized as non-integrated, partially integrated (enrolled in hospital-owned MA plan but operation at non-affiliated hospital), or fully integrated (operation at plan-owning hospital). Primary outcomes were elective operation volume and complication, with secondary outcomes of serious complication, length of stay, and ICU use. Multivariable linear models adjusted for patient factors and hospital/patient county effects. Results: Elective operations were 13.2% (p < 0.001) more likely to occur under full integration. Fully integrated admissions had significantly lower rate of any complication (-20 percent, (p < 0.001)) serious complication (-20.8 percent (p < 0.001)) ICU use (-13 percent (p < 0.001)) and shorter length of stay (-12.5 percent (p < 0.001)) compared with non-integrated admissions. Similar improvements were observed when compared with partially integrated admissions (Table 1). Conclusion: Hospital-MA VI is associated with improved postoperative outcomes, including fewer complications and shorter stay. rows.abstract: Application of the Risk Analysis Index to Elective Coronary Artery Bypass: A Nationwide Analysis Sean H Nguyen, MD, Lindsay L Welton, MD, Charles M Quinn, BS, Cole Myers, MD, Hilary Mosher, MFA, MD, James Harmon Jr, MD, PhD, FACS, Stephen J Huddleston, MD, PhD, FACS University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN; MercyOne Medical Center, Des Moines, IA; Minneapolis VAMC, Minneapolis, MN Introduction: The Risk Analysis Index (RAI) is a validated frailty index which, compared with other frailty measures, provides more granularity by grouping patients into Robust, Normal, Frail and Very Frail. Recently validated using ICD-10 codes, the RAI-ICD has yet to be applied at scale to coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). We hypothesized that compared with Normal, Robust patients undergoing elective CABG would have improved short-term outcomes, and Frail patients would have worse short-term outcomes. Methods: The National Inpatient Sample was queried to identify adults undergoing primary elective CABG (2016-2022). RAI-ICD scores were calculated using corresponding ICD-10 codes and grouped patients into Robust, Normal, Frail and Very Frail. Outcomes of mortality, non-home discharge, prolonged length of stay (LOS >14 days), and complication (cardiopulmonary, infectious, and renal) were compared. Results: A weighted total of 482,560 patients were included. Most were Robust (56%), followed by Normal (40%), Frail (3%), and Very Frail (1%). All cohorts differed in age, sex, race, primary payer, and patient location (p < 0.05). When compared with the Normal cohort, the Robust cohort had lower odds of inpatient mortality, non-home discharge, prolonged LOS, and complication (p < 0.001, Figure 1). Frail and Very Frail patients had higher odds of all adverse outcomes (p < 0.01). Adjusted models for mortality and non-home discharge displayed similar trends. Conclusion: Robustness is protective, while frailty is predictive of poorer outcomes. Implementation of RAI during elective CABG consultation may improve patient counseling and surgical planning.Figure 1Cerebral Perfusion During Hypothermic Circulatory Arrest: A Systematic Review of Neurocognitive Outcomes and Prevailing Practices Jessica B Briscoe, MD, Caroline A Tran, BS, Esteban A Molina, MD, Alyssia Venna, MBS, Samrawit De La Cruz, BS, Janelle Sangalang, BS, AlleaBelle Bradshaw, MD, Jennifer S Lawton, MD, FACS Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD; Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD; Medstar Georgetown-Washington Hospital Center, Washington, DC; Children’s National Hospital, Washington, DC; University of Arizona College of Medicine, Tucson, AZ Introduction: There is currently no consensus on the optimal strategy for neuroprotection during hypothermic circulatory arrest (HCA) during aortic operation. This systematic review summarizes neurocognitive outcomes after cardiac surgery using HCA with various strategies for cerebral protection to inform practice patterns and future clinical research. Methods: A systematic review was conducted of studies including adults undergoing HCA with cerebral perfusion and subsequent assessment of neurologic outcomes. Case reports, non-English articles, and pediatric populations were excluded. Results: A total of 1616 studies were identified. After screening and a full-text review of 198 studies, 82 articles were included in the final analysis (Figure 1); 64 were retrospective studies, 11 were prospective cohort studies, and 7 were randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The median sample size was 120 (interquartile range [IQR] 61, 324). A total of 67 studies evaluated outcomes such as permanent (PND) and temporary neurologic (TND) deficits and found no difference between cerebral perfusion strategies in PND, TND, or stroke. Six studies (n = 212) reported on neurocognition effects with antegrade cerebral perfusion and retrograde cerebral perfusion. Retrograde was associated with memory, attention, and processing deficits in 45% (33/73) of cases. Of the 7 RCTs, the median number of patients per study was 34, and few evaluated outcomes after 6 months. Conclusion: This review elucidates the wide range of practice strategies and underscores the need for high-volume, large randomized clinical trials to determine the optimal treatment for neuroprotection during HCA. The significant diversity in treatment approaches warrants clinical consensus and the development of a gold-standard technique.Figure 1Comparative Analysis of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement Outcomes in Patients with Previous Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting: A Propensity-Matched 10-Year Multinational Analysis Andrew F Ibrahim, BS, Masab Mansoor, DBA, Annmarie Farag, BS, Valeria S Levin, BS, Casey D Brusen, BS, Benjamin Hirsch, MD Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center School of Medicine, Lubbock, TX; John Sealy School of Medicine, Galveston, TX; Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center, Lubbock, TX Introduction: As the rate of coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) increases, a significant number of patients with a history of CABG require aortic valve replacement. The risks associated with repeat sternotomy in surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) are significant, compared with less invasive transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). This analysis looks to address the paucity of literature on outcomes of TAVR vs SAVR in patients with prior CABG. Methods: The TriNetX global federated database was queried for patients who underwent TAVR or SAVR with history of CABG. Propensity score matching was conducted to create comparable cohorts. Outcomes included mortality, stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA), permanent pacemaker placement (PPM), acute MI, acute kidney injury (AKI), heart failure (HF), and major bleeding within 1 year of valve replacement. Results: A total of 5,030 SAVR and 8,175 TAVR patients were identified before matching, with 3,373 matched pairs (Figure 1). Before matching, the TAVR cohort was older and had a significantly higher burden of comorbid conditions. After matching, these differences were mitigated. Compared with TAVR, post-CABG SAVR was significantly associated with higher odds of 1-year mortality (1.266, 95% CI 1.072-1.495, p = 0.005), stroke/TIA, acute MI, and AKI (Figure 1). In contrast, TAVR was associated with higher odds of HF and PPM. Major bleeding events were similar between TAVR and SAVR. Conclusion: In this multinational cohort of patients with prior CABG, TAVR was associated lower rate of 1-year mortality, stroke/TIA, MI, and AKI, but higher rate of HF and PPM as compared with SAVR.Figure 1Effects of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Introduction on Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement Patient Risk Score, Surgical Techniques, and Outcomes in a Veterans Affairs Healthcare System Neal Mukherjee, BA, BS, Salvador A Tello, BS, Aditya Dwivedi, BS, Yixuan Huang, BA, Joshua Z Xian, BS, Axel O Gomez, MD, William Carroway, MD, Marko Boskovski, MD, Liang Ge, PhD, Elaine E Tseng, MD, FACS University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA Introduction: Since FDA transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) approval in 2011, TAVR vs surgical AVR (SAVR) decision-making has been influenced by expanding FDA indications, evolving SAVR technology, and concerns for TAVR durability. Simultaneously, TAVR has influenced SAVR techniques such as the focus on implantation of larger valves. Here, we evaluate the impact on our hospital of TAVR introduction on SAVR practice including changes to risk profiles of SAVR patients, SAVR outcomes, and operative techniques. Methods: A total of 350+ SAVR patients since 2009 were reviewed for preoperative characteristics to calculate Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality (STS-PROM), postoperative outcomes relevant to Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC3) criteria, and operative techniques/technology. Data was compared between a pre-TAVR era from 1/1/2009 to 11/25/2013 (date of our first TAVR) and a post-TAVR era from 11/26/2013 to 6/24/2024. Results: Per Table 1, patient demographics were similar pre/post-TAVR. Post-TAVR STS-PROM operative mortality significantly decreased. Most acute VARC3 outcomes improved, with significant decrease in the frequency of acute bleeding requiring transfusion, mortality, and kidney injury. Additionally, Kaplan-Meier 5-year survival increased post-TAVR (p = 0.001). SAVR operative technique was also impacted post-TAVR with implanted valve sizes increasing (p < 0.001) and del-Nido cardioplegia becoming ubiquitous (p < 0.001). In Table 1, continuous variables are reported as mean with SD. Categorical variables are reported with count and percentages. Conclusion: Post-TAVR, fewer high-risk patients underwent SAVR with TAVR availability. Patients who did undergo SAVR experienced better mid-term outcomes with concurrent increase in surgical valve size.
